paragraphs.source_en: The use of hallucinogenic plants or mushrooms in the Round Head art has been proposed by Samorini (1989) who believes that scenes of masked dancing figures may be interpreted this way. This hypothesis has been elaborated upon by Soleilhavoup (1998; 2005; 2007). He uses the shamanistic-oriented approach applied by Lewis-Williams for the Southern African rock art, with scenes representing people presumably in a trance or during their passage from the ordinary into the non-ordinary reality (Lewis-Williams 1981; 2004). In the Round Head complex Soleilhavoup believes that he finds similar shamanistic scenes represented as "flying" or "floating" anthropomorphic figures, sometimes with extremely long limbs, which would represent a shaman during his or her way to the altered state of consciousness.

paragraphs.source_en: However, the shamanistic interpretation applied to the Central Saharan paintings has several insufficiencies. The presumed shamanistic scenes with "flying" figures and/or their long limbs are very rare in the Round Head art, so that this interpretation can only be applied to a very limited number of figures. The majority of the Round Head figures are represented in a static position without any allusion to possible altered states of consciousness. A large amount of figures are represented in movement which may indicate dancing. But is it reasonable to suppose that each dancing figure is the result of an altered state of consciousness? It is probably not the only interpretation as dancing in prehistoric societies could have had various reasons and purposes.

paragraphs.source_en: The other objection relates to the presumed shamanistic drums represented in the Round Head art. These objects, generally called "meduses" for their resemblance to jellyfish (see figure 3-6), have been interpreted as animal skins or masks (Sansoni 1994; Muzzolini 1995a), but their significance as drums (Soleilhavoup 2007) is not convincing. The Round Head anthropomorphic figures are never represented holding these objects or any other object resembling a drum, so that they cannot, in certainty, be considered as musical instruments. They are painted both in isolation or superimposed over anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figures.
